h1: Google Business Profile for Criminal Defense Lawyers: Setup, Reviews and the Map
nav_label: Google Business Profile for Defense Lawyers
lead: When someone is arrested, the first search often happens on a phone in a parking lot, a hallway or a kitchen at 2am. A family member types dui lawyer near me or criminal defense attorney in a county name, and Google shows three firms in the map before anything else. Those three firms get most of the calls. Your Google Business Profile is what puts your firm in that spot, and it is also where nervous people judge you in a few seconds. This guide is for criminal defense attorneys and firm owners who want to set up and run their profile properly: the right categories, practitioner profiles, photos and hours, the review problem that is unique to defense work, how to avoid and fix suspensions, and how to tell whether the profile is bringing in paying clients.
quick_answer: A Google Business Profile for a criminal defense lawyer is the free listing that shows your firm in Google Maps and the local map results, with your address, hours, phone number, reviews and photos. To make it work, use your real firm name with no added keywords, choose criminal justice attorney or a similar category as your main category, use a real staffed office address rather than a virtual office, keep your hours honest, and reply to every review without revealing anything about a client. Criminal defense firms often get fewer reviews because clients value privacy, so build a respectful, private review request into the end of every case. Track calls from the profile and which of them become retained clients.
takeaways: The Map Gets the First Calls.
People in a crisis call one of the first firms they see, and the map is often first.
No keywords in your name and no virtual offices. Both can get a profile suspended.
Your main category tells Google which searches you belong in.
Defense clients value discretion. Make leaving a review easy and optional.
Reply to reviews without saying who they are or what they were charged with.
Count calls from the profile that become paying clients, not just views.

sections.h2: What Is a Google Business Profile and Why Does It Matter for Defense Firms?
sections.answer: It is the free listing that shows your firm in Google Maps and in the map box at the top of local searches, and for defense firms it often brings the fastest calls of any marketing channel.
paras: A Google Business Profile, which used to be called Google My Business, is the panel that shows your firm name, star rating, reviews, address, hours, photos and a call button. It appears in Google Maps and in the group of three firms, often called the map pack, that sits near the top of searches like criminal lawyer near me.

Criminal defense is one of the most urgent kinds of legal search. People search right after an arrest, a court date notice or a call from a family member in jail. They are stressed, often on a phone, and they usually call one of the first firms that looks trustworthy. A strong profile puts you in front of them at that moment, without paying for each click.

The profile also works behind the scenes. Many people who hear about you from a friend or another lawyer will still search your firm name before calling, and your profile is usually the first thing they see. Our guide to [[a:local-seo-for-criminal-defense-lawyers|local SEO for criminal defense lawyers]] covers how the profile fits with your website and the rest of your local search work.

sections.h2: How Do You Set Up a Google Business Profile for a Criminal Defense Firm?
sections.answer: Create or claim the profile with your real firm name and staffed office address, choose your categories, add hours, phone and website, and verify it.
paras: Start by searching your firm name in Google Maps to see whether a profile already exists. Firms often find an old profile created years ago, sometimes with the wrong phone number or an outdated address. Claim that profile instead of creating a new one, because duplicate profiles can cause problems.

Enter your firm name exactly as it appears on your sign, letterhead and website. Add the address of the office where clients can meet you during your stated hours, your main phone number and a link to the most relevant page of your website. For a single-office firm, that is usually your home page or main criminal defense page.

Google offers several ways to verify a business, which can include a phone call, a text, an email, a video recording or a live video call, depending on what Google offers your profile. Have the office ready to show your signage, your office and proof that you work from that address if Google asks for a video.

Once verified, fill in everything that applies: hours, services, a short description of your practice, photos, and attributes such as wheelchair accessibility. A complete profile gives Google and clients more reasons to trust you.

sections.h2: Which Categories Should a Criminal Defense Lawyer Choose?
sections.answer: Choose the most accurate main category, usually criminal justice attorney, and add a small number of secondary categories that truly describe your work.
paras: Your main category is one of the strongest signals for which searches your profile can show up in. For most defense firms, criminal justice attorney is the closest match to what clients search for. Some firms that handle a lot of drink driving cases also add DUI attorney as a secondary category where it is available.

Secondary categories should describe real services you offer from that office. Adding unrelated categories, such as a family law category when you rarely take divorce cases, can confuse Google and the people who find you. Google's guidelines say categories should describe your business as a whole, not be used as keywords.

Check the categories your top local competitors use. You can see them on their profiles in Google Maps. This does not mean copying them, but it helps you understand which categories Google seems to link with defense searches in your area.

sections.h2: What Name and Address Rules Do Defense Lawyers Need to Know?
sections.answer: Use your real-world firm name with nothing added, and only list an address where you actually meet clients during your hours. These two rules cause more suspensions than anything else.
paras: It is tempting to name the profile something like Smith Law DUI Lawyer Phoenix, because keywords in the name can seem to help rankings. Google's guidelines say including unnecessary information in your business name is not permitted and could result in the suspension of your profile. If your sign and letterhead say Smith Law Firm, that is your profile name.

Addresses are just as strict. Google says P.O. boxes and mailboxes at remote locations are not acceptable, and that a virtual office, a rented address you do not operate from, is not eligible for a Business Profile. Many defense attorneys meet clients at the courthouse, at the jail or by phone, but a profile needs a real office with permanent signage where you can be reached during stated hours.

If you serve several counties, you do not need an office in each one to get cases there. Use your real office address, list the areas you serve, and build strong local pages on your website for each county or city. Opening fake offices to appear in more towns is one of the quickest ways to lose a profile.

sections.h2: Should Each Defense Attorney Have Their Own Profile?
sections.answer: Sometimes. Google treats lawyers as individual practitioners, so a public-facing attorney can have a profile, but a firm with several lawyers at one office also needs its own separate firm profile.
paras: Google's guidelines treat lawyers as individual practitioners, alongside doctors and financial planners. A practitioner can have their own profile if they work in a public-facing role and can be contacted directly at the verified location during stated hours. Support staff should not have their own profiles.

For a solo defense attorney whose firm is essentially them, one profile for the firm is usually enough. For a firm with several attorneys at one office, Google says the organization should have its own profile for that location, separate from any practitioner profiles.

Attorney profiles can help well-known lawyers who are searched by name, especially former prosecutors or attorneys with a strong local reputation. They also add work: each profile needs accurate details and review management. Start with a strong firm profile, then add attorney profiles where people already search for the lawyer by name.

sections.h2: How Should a Defense Firm Set Its Hours?
sections.answer: List the hours when a real person can answer your phone and, if you take after-hours calls, say so honestly in the profile.
paras: Arrests do not keep office hours. Many defense searches happen at night and on weekends, and Google tends to show profiles that are open when people search. That makes it tempting to list your firm as open 24 hours.

Only do that if someone actually answers. A family member who calls at midnight and reaches a full voicemail will often call the next firm on the list. If you have an answering service or an attorney on call, your hours can reflect that. If not, list your real office hours and use the description and your website to explain how to reach you after hours.
Keep holiday hours up to date as well. A profile that says open on a holiday when no one answers creates a bad first impression at the exact moment someone needs you.

sections.h2: Why Do Criminal Defense Firms Get Fewer Reviews?
sections.answer: Because many clients do not want their name publicly linked to a criminal case, even when they are very happy with the result.
paras: This is the biggest difference between defense and other practice areas. An injury client may be glad to tell the world that a firm helped them after a crash. A client whose charge was dismissed may never want their name and the words criminal lawyer on the same page, and their family may feel the same way.

That is normal and it should be respected. The goal is not to pressure anyone. It is to make sure the clients who are willing to leave a review are asked, at the right time, in a way that respects their privacy. Even a few reviews a month can make a big difference in defense, because many competitors have very few.

Reviews also matter more in defense than you might think. People choosing a defense lawyer are often scared and know nothing about lawyers. Reading that other people felt supported, kept informed and treated with respect helps them pick up the phone.

sections.h2: How Can a Defense Lawyer Ask for Reviews Without Making Clients Uncomfortable?
sections.answer: Ask privately at the end of the case, explain that a review can use initials or a first name, and make it completely optional.
paras: The best time to ask is when the case is resolved and the client is relieved, such as after a dismissal, a reduced charge or a good plea outcome. Ask in person or by phone first, then follow up with a short text or email with a direct link to your review page.

Let clients know they control what they share. A Google review shows the name on their Google account, so some clients may prefer to use an account with only their initials or first name, and they never need to mention their charge. A simple line such as you do not need to say anything about your case, just how we treated you, makes many clients more comfortable.

Never offer anything in return. Google says offering incentives in exchange for reviews is strictly prohibited, and most state bar rules do not let lawyers give anything of value for a recommendation. Never ask staff, friends or family to post reviews, and never write reviews yourself.

Families can be a good source of reviews too. A parent or spouse who hired you for a loved one often wants to thank you and may be more comfortable posting a review than the client is. The same rules apply: honest experience, no incentives.
list: Ask at the end of the case, when the client feels relieved
Use a direct link to your Google review page
Say they never need to mention their case or charge
Make it clearly optional, with no pressure and no reward
Thank every reviewer briefly in your reply

sections.h2: How Should You Reply to Reviews on a Defense Profile?
sections.answer: Thank people briefly and never confirm that anyone was a client or mention a charge, court or outcome.
paras: Replies are public and permanent. A reply that says glad we got your DUI dismissed, John confirms that John was charged with a DUI. That breaks client confidentiality and can embarrass a client who trusted you. Keep every reply general, even when the review itself shares details.

For positive reviews, a short thank you is enough, such as thank you for your kind words, we appreciate you taking the time to share your experience. For negative reviews, stay calm and general: say your firm takes all feedback seriously, that professional rules limit what you can discuss, and invite the person to contact the office directly.

Some negative reviews in defense come from people who are not clients at all, such as alleged victims, opposing parties or people angry at the system. You can report reviews that break Google's rules, but never reply in a way that argues about a case or reveals anything about it.

sections.h2: What Should Defense Firms Post and Add to Their Profile?
sections.answer: Real photos of your office and team, clear services, a short honest description and occasional updates that help people in a stressful moment.
paras: Photos build trust quickly. Add pictures of your office exterior and sign, which also help people find you, your reception area, and your attorneys. Real photos beat stock images every time.

Use the services section to list the main types of cases you handle, such as DUI, drug charges, assault, theft, domestic violence, juvenile cases and expungement, where your state allows the work. Keep each description short and plain.

Profile updates can share helpful, general information, such as what to do after an arrest, what happens at a first court date, or how bail works in your county. Avoid anything that sounds like a guaranteed outcome, and keep the bar's advertising rules in mind, because profile posts are part of your public marketing.

sections.h2: How Does a Defense Profile Rank in the Google Map?
sections.answer: Google says local results are mainly based on relevance, distance and popularity, so you need an accurate profile, a real nearby office and steady reviews.
paras: Google's own help page says local results are mainly based on relevance, distance and popularity. Relevance is how well your profile matches the search, which depends a lot on your categories, services and website. Distance is how far your office is from the person searching or the place they searched for. Popularity is how well known your firm is, which includes reviews, links and mentions across the web.

Distance is the one you cannot change without moving. A firm whose office is near the courthouse or in the county seat often shows up more for searches there. That is why genuine local pages on your website, and links from local organizations, matter so much for the areas a little further away.

Your website and your profile work together. A profile that links to a strong page about criminal defense in your county, with clear information about local courts and charges, usually does better than one that points to a thin page. Our guide to [[a:blog/seo-keywords-for-criminal-defense-lawyers|SEO keywords for criminal defense lawyers]] explains which local searches matter most.

sections.h2: Why Do Criminal Defense Profiles Get Suspended, and How Do You Fix It?
sections.answer: Most suspensions come from keywords in the name, virtual or shared addresses, duplicate profiles or sudden edits. If it happens, fix the cause and submit an appeal.
paras: Legal profiles are watched closely because spam is common in law. A suspended profile disappears from the map or loses the ability to be edited, which can cut calls overnight. The usual causes are keywords added to the business name, an address that is a virtual office or a shared co-working desk without proper signage, more than one profile for the same location, or many big changes made at once.

If your profile is suspended, do not create a new one. Google specifically warns against creating a new Business Profile for the same business. Instead, review the guidelines, correct anything that does not follow them, and gather proof such as photos of your sign and office, a lease or utility bill, and your bar registration showing the address.

If you believe your profile should be reinstated, you can submit an appeal through Google's appeals tool and add your evidence. Appeals can take time, so it pays to get the basics right from the start and to make big changes slowly and one at a time.

sections.h2: How Do You Know Whether Your Profile Is Bringing in Clients?
sections.answer: Watch calls, website clicks and direction requests from the profile, then match calls to retained clients.
paras: Your profile shows performance data such as how many people called, clicked to your website or asked for directions. Those numbers are useful, but the real question is how many of those people hired you.

Use a call tracking number in the profile's website link or ask every new client how they found you, and note it in your case management system. Over a few months you should be able to see how many retained clients came from the map and which charges they were for.

Look at timing as well. If many calls from the profile come late at night and go to voicemail, that is a sign your after-hours coverage is costing you clients. Our guide to [[a:criminal-defense-marketing|criminal defense marketing]] covers how the profile fits with your other channels.

sections.h2: A Note on Rules and Results
sections.answer: Google's policies and bar rules change, and every market is different.
paras: This article gives general information, not legal or ethics advice. Google updates its Business Profile guidelines and review policies from time to time, and state bar advertising and confidentiality rules vary. Check the current guidelines and your state's rules before making changes, and remember that rankings depend on many factors, including competition and where people are when they search.
